meta.title: Perennialism — Chronology
meta.subtitle: Chronology of the Traditionalist School as an intellectual movement (1921–present)
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of perennialism — the Traditionalist School of René Guénon, Ananda Coomaraswamy and Frithjof Schuon — as a movement of ideas: the books, the journals, the political adaptations and the reception, from the 1920s to the school's unexpected afterlife in 21st-century politics. The Maryamiyya order's initiatic history is the sibling project cronologia/tariqa.
meta.dataQualityNote: This is a work-in-progress dataset about a contested intellectual lineage whose political receptions are actively disputed. Every fact is cited; dates the sources dispute are flagged with a ? mark; and every characterization — above all about the Evola line, the alt-right reception, contested affiliations (Eliade) and living figures — is attributed to the scholar or actor making it, never asserted in the site's own voice. Corrections against published sources are welcome.

threads.note: These lanes are an editorial reading of this chronology, not a neutral index. Charting a school of IDEAS carries a risk the institutional chronologies do not: to periodize a body of thought is largely to periodize its RECEPTION, and how this school should be received is the contested question itself. So three things are stated rather than implied. There is no lane splitting 'the school' from 'its critics' — that division would manufacture a symmetry the sources do not support. The lane holding the political line is labelled as disputed, because whether Evola belongs INSIDE this school or among its appropriations is precisely what the sources argue about, and a lane cannot be allowed to settle it by filing. And the reception lanes hold READINGS, which the dataset's own titles already mark as such ('Read as concealment…', "the 'islamization' reading"). Events belong to several lanes where they belong to several storylines. What was considered and left out, and why, is recorded on issue #46.

lanes.label: The school's own authors and works
lanes.basis: The books, journals and authorial events this chronology records as the school's own output — Guénon, Coomaraswamy, Schuon, Burckhardt, Pallis, Lings, Nasr, Études Traditionnelles and Temenos — together with the biographical moments that bear on that output (Cairo 1930, the deaths of 1947 and 1951). Membership here follows what the dataset already presents as the school's corpus; it is not a judgement about who is a 'real' Traditionalist.

lanes.label: The political line (its place in the school is disputed)
lanes.basis: Evola's works and trial, Dugin, and the Bannon episode. The lane exists because this dataset records a DOCUMENTED FAULT LINE, not because we have decided the question: Guénon's 1929 assertion of the sacerdotal over the royal and Evola's 1934 inversion of it are in the record as an explicit disagreement, and 1929 therefore carries this lane as well as the school's. Whether Evola is inside the school or among its appropriations is argued in the sources; the label says the placement is disputed so the lane cannot be read as settling it.

lanes.label: Reception and study, as readings
lanes.basis: How others read, studied, taught and honoured the school: academic treatments (Sedgwick 2004 and 2023, Hanegraaff 2012), a Catholic review carrying Guénon in 1925, teaching reach (Smith 1958), a Gifford lectureship, and elite reception (the Sacred Web address and 'Harmony'). These are readings, not verdicts, and the dataset's own event titles already mark them as readings — the lane keeps that framing rather than flattening them into findings.

lanes.label: The Brazilian reception
lanes.basis: The Carvalho material — the 2001 Montfort exchange, the Curso Online de Filosofia readings of 2009–2014, the 2016 programmatic statement, and the 2022 Brazilian translations. This is reception too, and it is separated from the reception lane only because it is by far this repo's largest and most finely dated strand, not because it is a different kind of act. Each entry is a reading attributed to its author, several of which the dataset records him advancing and elsewhere qualifying.

lanes.label: Adjacent coinages and parallels
lanes.basis: Terms and currents that share this school's vocabulary or people without being its work: Steuco's 1540 coinage of philosophia perennis, four centuries earlier and for a different thesis; Huxley's 1945 bestseller under the same phrase; and the organic-farming coinage that came out of the 1939 Betteshanger school. Grouping them says they are adjacent, and the lane exists so that adjacency is visible rather than being mistaken for lineage.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: The [[traditionalist-school|Traditionalist School]]: the current of thought founded by René Guénon and developed by Ananda Coomaraswamy and Frithjof Schuon, holding that all orthodox religions transmit one primordial, perennial truth — and that modernity is the story of its loss.

facts.label: Founding corpus
facts.value: Guénon's books of 1921–1945, from the 'Introduction générale' to 'The Reign of Quantity'; Coomaraswamy's metaphysical essays after 1932; Schuon's 'The Transcendent Unity of Religions' (1948).

facts.label: House journal
facts.value: Études Traditionnelles (Paris, 1936–1992) — the renamed Le Voile d'Isis (founded 1889), dominated by Guénon and his school for over half a century.

facts.label: The two lines
facts.value: Schuon's religious-metaphysical line (which organized as the Maryamiyya order — see the sibling tariqa project) and Julius Evola's political-heroic adaptation, whose postwar radical-right reception runs to Dugin, the alt-right and the Bannon episode — every link in that chain attributed.

facts.label: The name's traps
facts.value: '[[philosophia-perennis|Perennial philosophy]]' predates and exceeds the school: Steuco coined it in 1540, Leibniz reused it, neo-Scholastics applied it to Thomism, and Aldous Huxley's 1945 bestseller made it mean a universalist mysticism the Guénonians rejected. This site is about the Guénonian school; the others appear only for disambiguation.

facts.label: Scholarship
facts.value: Mark Sedgwick's 'Against the Modern World' (2004) and 'Traditionalism' (2023) are the academic backbone; Wouter Hanegraaff situates the school critically within the study of Western esotericism; Benjamin Teitelbaum's 'War for Eternity' (2020) covers the political chapter — with reviewers disputing how coherent that network really is.

events.title: Steuco coins 'philosophia perennis'
events.text: Agostino Steuco's 'De perenni philosophia' introduces the term — for a continuity thesis inside Christian Platonism, centuries before and apart from the Guénonian school.

events.title: Guénon's first books
events.text: 'Introduction générale à l'étude des doctrines hindoues' frames 'Tradition' against modernity; 'Le Théosophisme' separates the school-to-be from occultism and Theosophy.

events.title: 'L'Erreur spirite'
events.text: Guénon's companion polemic against Spiritism completes the boundary-drawing against the occult milieu.

events.title: 'Orient et Occident'
events.text: Guénon's program for a Western elite reoriented by Eastern metaphysics — and his break with the Catholic intellectuals among whom he had first written.

events.title: 'L'Homme et son devenir selon le Vêdânta'
events.text: Guénon's central metaphysical exposition, published in 1925 by Bossard (Paris) — confirmed against the French Wikipedia bibliographic record and Zoccatelli's CESNUR study, which both date the first edition to 1925; the '1927' of a derived source was an error.

events.title: The Regnabit episode
events.text: Regnabit — revue universelle du Sacré-Cœur, founded in June 1921 by Fr. Félix Anizan OMI, carries nineteen Guénon articles between August/September 1925 and May 1927, the symbolist scholar Louis Charbonneau-Lassay having recruited him — the high point of his attempted rapprochement with Catholic milieux. Guénon's 12-page letter of 8 June 1928 to Charbonneau-Lassay closes the episode; Guénon blamed 'the hostility of some neo-scholastic milieus' (his framing), while Zoccatelli's study documents intra-congregational controversies around Anizan's Sacred Heart theology from 1923.

events.title: 'La Crise du monde moderne'
events.text: The school's most-read statement of civilizational critique — the template for all its later 'crisis' literature.

events.title: 'Autorité spirituelle et pouvoir temporel'
events.text: Guénon asserts the priority of the sacerdotal over the royal — the doctrinal fault line that would divide him from Evola.

events.title: Guénon settles in Cairo
events.text: He writes thereafter as a Muslim while addressing a mainly French readership, until his death in 1951.

events.title: Coomaraswamy's metaphysical turn
events.text: The Boston Museum of Fine Arts curator shifts from art history to studies of tradition, myth and metaphysics — the essays of 1932–1947 make him the school's comparativist of 'traditional art', Vedanta and Platonism.

events.title: Evola's 'Revolt Against the Modern World'
events.text: Julius Evola's political-heroic adaptation of Traditionalism subordinates the priestly to the regal — against Guénon's 1929 position; Guénon's review rejected key theses while granting the work's interest.

events.title: Schuon's first book, 'Leitgedanken zur Urbesinnung'
events.text: Frithjof Schuon's first book — written in German, completed in 1932 and published in 1935, later translated into English as 'Primordial Meditation: Contemplating the Real' — precedes 'The Transcendent Unity of Religions' (1948) by thirteen years. The place of publication is not recorded here. The title does not appear in the French-language bibliography on the official Schuon site, which begins at 1948; the 1935 date rests on the encyclopedia entry.

events.title: 'Études Traditionnelles' is born
events.text: Le Voile d'Isis (founded 1889) is renamed Études Traditionnelles, reflecting Guénon's dominance of the review — the school's house journal until 1992, with a wartime gap 1940–45.

events.title: Evola's racial doctrine, and what it did and did not amount to
events.text: Between the 1938 racial laws and 1941 the political line of Traditionalism acquires an explicitly racial doctrine, and this chronology records it because the gap between 'Revolt Against the Modern World' (1934) and the 1951 trial would otherwise read as a silence. Per the encyclopedia record, writings by Evola in the late 1930s contributed arguments for Fascist Italy's repression of its Jews, and he encouraged and applauded Mussolini's antisemitic racial laws of 1938; in 'Sintesi di dottrina della razza' (Synthesis of the Doctrine of Race, 1941) he set out his ideas on race and eugenics and introduced the notion of a 'spiritual racism' ranking a race of the spirit above one of the body, a book the same record says was endorsed by Mussolini. Evola also said he had worked for the Sicherheitsdienst, the SS intelligence service — an account given by him, recorded here as his own statement rather than as an independently documented appointment. Two distinctions the sources will not let this entry blur. First, contributing arguments for the persecution, and applauding laws once made, is not the same as drafting them: no source consulted here places Evola among the authors of the 1938 measures, and the stronger claim in circulation that he helped form the racial laws is not carried. Second, none of this is Guénon's line: the doctrinal split recorded at 1929 and 1934 is what separates them, and Guénon's own reception has no equivalent chapter. The characterizations are the cited sources', dated and attributed.

events.title: 'Peaks and Lamas'
events.text: Marco Pallis's best-selling mountaineering-and-Buddhism book carries a Traditionalist reading of Tibet to a wide audience.

events.title: The Betteshanger Summer School — where the organic coinage came from
events.text: Lord Northbourne hosts the Betteshanger Summer School and Conference on Bio-Dynamic Farming at his farm in Kent, 1–9 July 1939: a nine-day course for British farmers given by Ehrenfried Pfeiffer, who travelled from Switzerland, supported by the biodynamic practitioners Otto Eckstein and Hans Heinze, with Dr Scott Williamson of the Peckham Experiment as the only British lecturer. Northbourne had gone to Switzerland in January 1939 to arrange the visit, having already worked with Pfeiffer on the Farleigh Experiment in 1938; attendance was capped at forty and by invitation only. War broke out less than eight weeks later, and 'Look to the Land' followed in May 1940. This entry exists to keep the next one honest. John Paull's reconstruction — the source for all of the above — argues that Betteshanger is the missing link between biodynamics and organic farming, that a direct line runs from Rudolf Steiner via Pfeiffer to Northbourne, and that 'Look to the Land' took the Steinerian view of the farm as an organism as its central tenet and made it the nominative motif of 'organic' farming, in an account offered to the Anglophone world secularized and at a distance from its Anthroposophical roots. So the coinage this chronology calls the school's most unexpected export has a documented immediate provenance that is not Traditionalist at all: it is Steiner's anthroposophy, a current the Traditionalist authors treated as precisely the kind of modern pseudo-initiatic movement they wrote against. Northbourne's later Traditionalism and his translations of Guénon and Burckhardt are real and are recorded elsewhere here; what this entry denies is the shortcut that reads 'organic farming' as an application of Traditionalist metaphysics. The characterizations are Paull's, dated and attributed.

events.title: 'Look to the Land' coins 'organic farming'
events.text: Lord Northbourne — later a Traditionalist author and translator of Guénon — introduces the term 'organic farming', framing agriculture as a clash of worldviews; long described here as the school's most unexpected export. The description needs one qualification, added after reading John Paull's account of the Betteshanger Summer School Northbourne had hosted eleven months earlier: on that reconstruction the book's central image of the farm as an organism is Steinerian and reaches Northbourne through Ehrenfried Pfeiffer's biodynamics, not through Guénon. Northbourne's Traditionalist authorship and his translations come later; the coinage is not an application of them.

events.title: 'The Reign of Quantity'
events.text: Guénon's summa on modernity as the reign of quantity is published in the Liberation moment.

events.title: Huxley's other 'Perennial Philosophy'
events.text: Aldous Huxley's bestselling anthology (Harper & Brothers, New York, 1945; Chatto & Windus, London, 1946) popularizes the phrase in a universalist-mystical sense — indifferent to orthodoxy and initiation — that the Guénonians rejected as syncretism. Same words, different lineage.

events.title: 'The Transcendent Unity of Religions'
events.text: Schuon's classic statement of the transcendent unity of religions (French 'De l'unité transcendante des religions', 1948; English translation by Peter Townsend, Faber and Faber, 1953 — not 1957); T. S. Eliot: 'I have met with no more impressive work in the comparative study of Oriental and Occidental religion.'

events.title: Evola tried and acquitted
events.text: Arrested as alleged ideologue of the neofascist FAR, Evola declares himself 'superfascista' while denying party fascism, and is acquitted — the trial that fixes his postwar political persona.

events.title: 'Sacred Art in East and West'
events.text: Titus Burckhardt's canonical Traditionalist theory of sacred art across five traditions (English translation by Lord Northbourne).

events.title: 'The Religions of Man'
events.text: Huston Smith's textbook (later 'The World's Religions') dominates American comparative-religion teaching; his openly perennialist 'Forgotten Truth' (1976) follows under Schuon's influence.

events.title: 'Understanding Islam'
events.text: Schuon's most popular book (French 'Comprendre l'Islam', Gallimard, 1961; English 1963) becomes a key channel of perennialism into Islamic studies. The 1961 first edition is confirmed by the official Schuon bibliography and Gallimard.

events.title: Evola's postwar canon
events.text: 'Men Among the Ruins' (1953) and 'Ride the Tiger' (1961) join 'Revolt' as the canon of the postwar Italian radical right, of which scholarship describes Evola as chief ideologue.

events.title: 'Logic and Transcendence'
events.text: Schuon's fullest engagement with modern philosophy (French 'Logique et transcendance', Les Éditions Traditionnelles, 1970; English 1975). The 1970 French first edition is confirmed by the official Schuon bibliography.

events.title: 'Temenos' launches
events.text: Kathleen Raine, Keith Critchlow, Brian Keeble and Philip Sherrard found the review devoted to 'the arts of the imagination' — seed of the Temenos Academy (1990), of which the Prince of Wales (now King Charles III) has been patron since its founding.

events.title: Nasr's Gifford Lectures
events.text: Seyyed Hossein Nasr delivers the Gifford Lectures, published as 'Knowledge and the Sacred' — per the Gifford records, the first Muslim and first non-Westerner to do so: the school's academic high-water mark.

events.title: Lings's 'Muhammad'
events.text: Martin Lings's prize-winning biography becomes the school's biggest crossover into mainstream Islamic readership.

events.title: 'Études Traditionnelles' ends
events.text: The school's flagship journal closes with the October–December 1992 issue, after a 1936–1992 run.

events.title: The Anglophone republication of Evola
events.text: The route by which Evola reached an English-speaking readership is a publishing history, and it is worth recording because the political reception this chronology tracks from 2017 onward runs through it. Inner Traditions International issued 'Revolt Against the Modern World' in English in 1995, per the edition record. The larger programme is now Arktos's: consulted on 30 July 2026, its own author listing carries twenty-four Evola titles, more than any other author on its list — ahead of Alexander Dugin at twenty-two and Guillaume Faye at twenty-one. That the same catalogue is the main Anglophone vehicle for both Evola and Dugin is a fact about the publisher's list, recorded here as such and not as a claim that the two bodies of work belong together. Arktos is a publisher of the European New Right and identitarian milieu, so on this question it is a participant in the reception rather than an observer of it, and its catalogue is cited only for its own composition. One limitation, stated rather than papered over: the storefront does not publish per-title release dates, so this republication wave is recorded by its endpoints and its present scale, and not as the series of dated releases the epic asked for. Closing that would need publisher records the public catalogue does not expose.

events.title: The Carvalho-Fedeli exchange on Guénon
events.text: In letters of 28 and 30 January 2001, published by the traditionalist-Catholic Associação Cultural Montfort, Olavo de Carvalho defends René Guénon against Orlando Fedeli's charge of gnosticism: the spiritual elevation Guénon shows 'in numerous passages of his work', he writes, is enough to inhibit any disrespectful contestation, and Guénon's relation to Christianity cannot be reduced to that of an infiltrator in Catholic circles. He also faults Fedeli's source, Marie-France James's 'Ésotérisme et christianisme' (1981), as having 'investigated so remotely, through indirect testimony', and says James treats Martin Lings and Lings's own pen-name Sidi Abu Bakr as two people. Fedeli's reply of 3 February 2001 presses him on whether he is himself Catholic. Both positions are the correspondents' own, not this site's. The exchange dates the Brazilian reception: Carvalho was still publicly defending Guénon in 2001, fifteen years before the 2016 'As garras da Esfinge' reversed that position — when he left Schuon's order is an order-side question and belongs to the sibling cronologia/tariqa project.

events.title: 'Against the Modern World'
events.text: Mark Sedgwick publishes the first full history of the movement — the academic backbone of this site.

events.title: The Prince of Wales addresses the Sacred Web conference
events.text: The Sacred Web conference on 'Tradition in the Modern World' meets at the Myer Horowitz Theatre, University of Alberta, Edmonton, on 23–24 September 2006, and opens with an introduction from the Prince of Wales — the future King Charles III — who says in it that he cannot be present, so the address is given in absentia and also exists as a video. It is the fullest public statement of his reading in this field, and unusually for this subject it is first-person rather than commentary. In it he speaks of the need for those who can speak of the eternal wisdom that is called the perennial philosophy; says he is always delighted to receive the latest issue of Sacred Web; states that through the work of the Temenos Academy, of which he is Patron, he has been fortunate to enjoy the writings of Seyyed Hossein Nasr and the late Martin Lings; notes that Temenos remains closely associated with many who write for Sacred Web, for Sophia and for related journals; and refers to the critique of the false premises of modernity set out in 'The Reign of Quantity'. Mark Sedgwick, writing on 1 October 2006, took the speech to show the Prince better read in Traditionalism than he had thought, and recorded that it nonetheless did not otherwise clarify his own personal position — which is the standard this chronology keeps. What the address establishes is reading, patronage and public praise, all self-disclosed; it establishes no membership, initiation or affiliation, and none is claimed here. The later commentary reads it the same way: Rod Dreher in The American Conservative (12 March 2012) calls him a devotee of the perennial philosophy on the strength of his public statements, and Theo Hobson in The Spectator (17 September 2022) places his outlook close to the perennial philosophy partly inspired by René Guénon — and neither asserts that he belongs to anything.

events.title: Dugin's 'Fourth Political Theory'
events.text: Aleksandr Dugin's post-liberal ideology (English translation 2012) draws explicitly on Traditionalism, making him the key conduit of its vocabulary into Russian geopolitics — an Evolian-line reception, attributed as such.

events.title: Read as concealment: the Traditionalist School in the Curso Online de Filosofia
events.text: Through the first three years of Olavo de Carvalho's Curso Online de Filosofia the school is treated as a body of thought whose defect, on his account, is not error but concealment — and the position is already fully formed in aula 005 (25 April 2009), three months before aula 015. Asked by a student whether Coomaraswamy, Guénon, Schuon and Evola fell into the same cognitive trap as Descartes, he answers that the trouble with the Traditionalist school is not cognitive but a matter of untruth: they are, he says, profound thinkers who speak on behalf of secret societies and so cannot tell the whole story, which is why a reader needs historical as well as imaginative equipment to reconstruct what is withheld. In the same lecture he separates the metaphysical Orient Guénon invokes from the historical one; notes that Guénon denounces the historical method while using it throughout Le Théosophisme; objects that the initiation Guénon's remedy relies on is an idealized Masonry rather than the historical one; reads the Sphinx pen-name as a demand to be deciphered rather than followed; argues that Guénon writes Eastern doctrine in the most characteristically French academic manner, so that reading Descartes is a prerequisite for reading him; and sets one prediction he counts right, the disappearance of cash, beside one he counts wrong, that China would never turn Bolshevik — a pairing he makes again in aula 146 (17 March 2012). By aula 131 (19 November 2011) the same charge is pressed with the transmission named. He rejects Guénon's account of symbolism as a primitive science preserved and handed on by esoteric organizations, on the ground that a natural symbolism could not be anyone's property; repeats Henri Massis's jibe that Guénon is wrapped up in his manvantaras; says he still cannot draw the line between where Guénon fails to understand and where he understands and conceals; and asks whether the shaykh he names as Guénon's initiator, Elish El-Kebir, did not have his own project of islamizing the West. Both lectures are Carvalho's characterization of the school, dated and attributed, and are recorded here as reception, never in this site's voice. Both are community transcriptions that have not been checked against the audio, so everything above is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: The 'islamization' reading stated in the Curso Online de Filosofia
events.text: The reading that casts Guénon and Schuon as pioneers of an islamization of the West is already stated in Olavo de Carvalho's Curso Online de Filosofia seven years before the 2016 Verbum article that gave it its programmatic form. In aula 015 (18 July 2009) he tells the course that he had written an article describing René Guénon and Frithjof Schuon as pioneers of that process, that many people had demanded proof, and that his answer was that he has no proof — he is a witness, he was there and he saw, and he cannot prove it. That is the reading's evidentiary basis in its author's own words, and the reason this chronology carries it as reception rather than as finding. In aula 041 (16 January 2010) he puts it in its strongest form: that Schuon, returning from Algeria as shaykh of the tariqa of Shaykh al-Alawi, declared he would islamize the West, and that Guénon called the founding of Schuon's order at Lausanne the only real effect his own teaching had ever had — from which Carvalho infers that islamization was Guénon's aim too. In the same lecture he reads out and endorses a passage holding Guénon fallible and, in his youthful writings, intellectually dishonest, against those who celebrate him as an infallible compass, and citing Louis de Maistre's 'L'Énigme René Guénon'. The inference, the characterization and the reading are Carvalho's, and are recorded here as dated reception, not as the site's voice. His account of what he saw inside Schuon's order is order-side testimony and belongs to the sibling cronologia/tariqa project. Both lectures are community transcriptions that have not been checked against the audio, so everything above is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: The transcendent unity of religions granted, and bounded
events.text: The same course that carries Carvalho's 'islamization' reading also carries his assent to the doctrinal claim at the centre of the school, and the two run side by side without either displacing the other. In aula 028 (17 October 2009), answering a student on gnosis in Hans Jonas and Voegelin against gnosis in Schuon, he says that much of what Guénon and Schuon teach is compatible with Christianity and with the other religions insofar as they keep to a core of metaphysical knowledge genuinely common to them, and that the two said and proved that such a common set of metaphysical principles exists; his own objection, he insists, is not Orlando Fedeli's charge of gnosticism, which he says does not impress him. In aula 038 (26 December 2009) he states the limit: a common metaphysics does exist across the traditions and Guénon and Schuon proved it, but metaphysics is a description of the structure of reality and is therefore not religion; the religions promise something beyond that description and diverge precisely there; no standpoint stands above the set of them; and the same common metaphysics is also found outside religion altogether, in Aristotle, Plato and al-Fārābī. In aula 101 (9 April 2011) he names Schuon's transcendent unity of religions and calls the theory correct while reading it narrowly, as asserting only that the metaphysical doctrine underlying the religions is the same, and points to Whitall Perry's compilation for the documentation. In aula 151 (21 April 2012) the position has its settled form: all the religions have the same metaphysics, but metaphysics is a schema of reality and says nothing about God's action in time, which is where he locates Christianity's difference. Across those three years the assent does not move while the polemic sharpens — which is what a five-year course can show and a single clip cannot. This is Carvalho's reading, attributed and dated; the lectures are community transcriptions unchecked against the audio, so everything here is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: 'Harmony' and the royal reception
events.text: The Prince of Wales publishes 'Harmony: A New Way of Looking at Our World'; commentators — Sedgwick, Commonweal — read Traditionalist and Nasrian influence in it, though the book cites no Traditionalist sources. Reported strictly as attributed reception, never as affiliation.

events.title: Credit where he gives it: the school's expositors acknowledged in the Curso Online de Filosofia
events.text: Alongside the concealment charge and the 'islamization' reading, the same course carries a steady line of dated, specific credit to the school's authors, and the two lines run together without either cancelling the other. In aula 040 (9 January 2010) Carvalho credits Guénon, Titus Burckhardt and Jean Borella with having restored the capacity to perceive the symbolic nature of reality, objecting in the same breath that by their method everything becomes symbol and one arrives only at an impersonal God. In aula 057 (8 May 2010) — the same year he presses the islamization charge — he says he cannot deny that the whole reconquest of the symbolic understanding of the universe came to the West by the Islamic route, through the Sufi turuq, Guénon and Schuon, and that thanks are owed. In aula 163 (14 July 2012) he recommends Schuon's L'Œil du Cœur and calls Schuon a great expositor of these matters even while under suspicion in other respects — the assent and the polemic in a single sentence. In aula 203 (11 May 2013) he credits Schuon with settling the question of whether logic binds God, citing Schuon's formulation of logic as the ontology of the microcosm that is human reason. In aula 211 (13 July 2013) he calls Schuon the coiner of the term 'transcendent unity of religions' and its most eloquent expositor, grants that the demonstration is irrefutable at the level of shared metaphysical principles, restates that a religion is not a metaphysical doctrine but a way of transformation and salvation whose differences live at that level — and adds that Schuon died leaving the resulting impasse unsolved (religions identical at the doctrinal summit yet neither interchangeable nor mixable), saying he does not know the solution either. All of this is Carvalho's dated, attributed reception; the lectures are community transcriptions unchecked against audio, so everything here is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: Carvalho's objection to Guénon's 'metaphysical realization'
events.text: In aula 088 (18 December 2010) and aula 092 (29 January 2011) Carvalho states at length the objection he elsewhere says is the fundamental one he holds against Guénon's doctrine. Guénon, on his summary, faults Western civilization and Christianity for stopping at salvation and missing metaphysical realization — the individual's dissolution into Brahman as the supreme universal reality. Carvalho answers that a realization which extinguishes the individual would make creation gratuitous, and that the accounts he credits of consciousness persisting in cardiac arrest report a surviving biographical self rather than an absorption; on the Christian view, he argues, individual souls are the most important thing in the universe and were not made to be reabsorbed, so there is no perspective superior to salvation. In aula 092 he adds the argument from acquaintance — that of the metaphysically realized men he has known, none resembled God or did anything divine — and says the doctrine of the multiple states of being is full of holes beneath an impression of total rigour. The claim to have known them is participant-witness testimony about the order and belongs to the sibling cronologia/tariqa project; what is recorded here is the doctrinal objection. It is Carvalho's argument, attributed and dated, not this site's; the lectures are community transcriptions unchecked against the audio, so everything above is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: The Carvalho–Dugin debate as a contest over the Traditionalist inheritance
events.text: The 2011 public exchange between Olavo de Carvalho and Aleksandr Dugin is worked through at length in the Curso Online de Filosofia, and what the lectures show is two readers disputing the same inheritance. Dugin, in text Carvalho reads out in aula 105, says he had expected to find in Carvalho a representative of the Brazilian Traditionalist philosophers in the line of René Guénon and Julius Evola, and reports having revised the Guénonian-Evolian anticommunism of his youth after the fall of communism, on the view that Soviet society was a parody of Tradition and still preferable to its total absence in the modern and postmodern world. Carvalho's replies contest the appropriation rather than the authors. In aula 099 (26 March 2011) he turns Guénon's own reign-of-quantity argument and the caste scheme he and Evola use against Dugin's holism, arguing that a collectivity is not a transcendent authority and that the Eurasian project is the opposite of a traditional society; he also notes that a Brazilian Catholic writer had dismissed him and Dugin together as Guénonians unable to see grace in history. In aula 105 he argues that Guénon's counter-initiation geography — the seven towers of the devil, none of them in the West and two in the Urals — cannot be made to license an anti-Western Eurasianism, and that Guénon sought to save the West rather than destroy it: his priority was the restoration of the Catholic Church, with an Islamic cultural revolution led by Sufi shaykhs over the Western intelligentsia as a secondary alternative and war and chaos as the consequence of both failing. That three-alternative structure is the same one Carvalho would publish in 2016 in 'As garras da Esfinge', five years earlier and in his own classroom. In aula 106 he characterizes Dugin's position as a crossing of Traditionalism with Bolshevism, and recommends Guénon's Le Théosophisme as the best critical revision of modern occultism while adding that its author has agendas of his own. This is the Evolian and political line of reception and is recorded separately from the religious and initiatic thread this dataset keeps distinct from it. Aulas 105 and 106 carry header dates of 7 May and 4 May 2011 respectively — a mutual three-day inversion, one of a small set of header-date inconsistencies the projects' dating review has measured across the corpus — so the week is settled but the order of the two lectures within it is not; the range above holds either way. Every characterization is Dugin's or Carvalho's, attributed and dated, never this site's; the lectures are community transcriptions unchecked against the audio, so everything above is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: Hanegraaff's 'Esotericism and the Academy'
events.text: Wouter Hanegraaff's study treats Traditionalism critically as 'religionism' within the academic history of Western esotericism.

events.title: Carvalho denies having introduced Guénon and Evola to Brazil
events.text: In aula 206 of the Curso Online de Filosofia (1 June 2013) Olavo de Carvalho rejects the claim, which he attributes to his own Wikipedia entry, that he introduced the works of René Guénon and Julius Evola to Brazil. On his account, translations of both authors and an active Guenonian circle had existed in Brazil for some forty years before him, and he counts himself the last to arrive on that scene. In the same answer he calls Evola a genius but mentally unbalanced and advises his students against reading him without long prior formation. The denial is a first-person correction to a widely repeated statement about the ideas' arrival in Brazil; his counter-claims — the decades of prior translations, the pre-existing Guenonian circle — are his own account, corroborated nowhere in this dataset's sources, and are recorded as attributed testimony, not as a finding about the Brazilian reception. The lecture is a community transcription not checked against audio; everything above is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: Guénon's French Catholic reception, as told in the Curso Online de Filosofia
events.text: Answering a student on the influence of the transcendent-unity idea over ecumenism, in aula 225 (26 October 2013) Carvalho describes Guénon's influence on French intellectual and especially Catholic milieux from the 1920s as profound but rarely acknowledged in public. He holds up Xavier Accart's monograph 'Guénon ou le renversement des clartés' (Édidit/Archè, 2005) as the documentation of that influence; points to Guénon's debate with Jean Daniélou, part of which he says is available in the Brazilian translation 'Sobre o Mistério da História'; and claims that Joseph Ratzinger, while a cardinal, credited Daniélou and Guénon with having turned the study of symbolism into a scientific field. The Ratzinger attribution is Carvalho's: no primary Ratzinger text was located when this entry was made — an endorsement of similar wording circulates in publisher material for Guénon's 'Symboles de la Science sacrée', without a citation — so it is carried here only as his claim, not as a fact about Ratzinger. In the same answer he restates the narrow assent the course had held since 2009: the transcendent-unity theory is correct insofar as it asserts a metaphysics common to the great religions, with Whitall Perry's anthology as the documentation, while salvation depends on divine action and lies outside what that common metaphysics covers. The lecture is a community transcription not checked against audio; everything above is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: Guénon's theory of initiation read against the Catholic sacraments
events.text: In aula 246 (19 April 2014) Carvalho expounds, and in part rejects, Guénon's theory of initiation as applied to Christianity. He states Guénon's thesis that Christianity began as an initiatic organization which, for want of valid religious institutions around it, externalized itself into a popular religion — and rejects it on the ground that Christ declared he had taught nothing in secret. He allows that the sacraments are, in Guénon's vocabulary, the Christian initiation, invoking John Paul II's description of baptism as the beginning of Christian initiation, while insisting that the initiation/esoterism grid fits the Islamic world — where the tariqas stand as distinct initiatic organizations beside a common popular religion — and not Christianity, where the rites are the same for everyone and only the depth of participation differs. Later in the lecture he restates Guénon's doctrine that an initiation received is virtual until effectuated and may remain virtual for a lifetime. All of this is reception of Guénon's doctrine of initiation; Carvalho's own initiatic history is order-side material and lives in the sibling cronologia/tariqa project. The lecture is a community transcription not checked against audio; everything above is paraphrase and nothing is quoted.

events.title: 'As garras da Esfinge' — the 'islamization' reading
events.text: Olavo de Carvalho publishes in Verbum (Ano I, nos. 1 e 2, Julho-Outubro de 2016) the programmatic statement of the reading that casts Guénon as an agent of Islam in the West: on his argument the labyrinth of impossibilities has one exit — 'o catolicismo só pode ser devolvido à sua integridade originária se consentir em submeter-se ao guiamento de mestres islâmicos. Ou isso, ou a ocupação do Ocidente pelos muçulmanos. Tertium non datur.' The same article grants that Guénon and his continuators made 'várias contribuições valiosas até mesmo à compreensão do catolicismo pelos próprios intelectuais católicos, especialmente no que concerne ao simbolismo e à arte sacra'. It reads the 1925-1927 Regnabit articles as proving only that Guénon still hoped to steer the Catholic Church 'por meio da persuasão gentil e da infiltração', and his 1930 departure for Egypt as the moment that hope is abandoned. The reading is Carvalho's and is contested; it is recorded here as reception, never as the site's voice. One of its supporting details is wrong: the article has Guénon marrying a daughter of Sheikh Elish El-Kebir, whereas the standard account has him marry Fatima Ibrahim, daughter of Sheikh Mohammad Ibrahim, in 1934, and never meet Elish El-Kebir, who had died.

events.title: The Bannon–Evola episode
events.text: After Steve Bannon's 2014 Vatican-conference remarks referencing Dugin and 'what's called the traditionalist movement', the New York Times' 'Steve Bannon Cited Italian Thinker Who Inspired Fascists' makes Evola and Traditionalism briefly front-page news, amid the alt-right republication of Evola. Interviewed by UnHerd on 28 July 2023, Mark Sedgwick set narrower limits than the news cycle had: on his account Bannon says that discovering Guénon was a turning point in his life, but not that it was the final one; he accepts parts of the Traditionalist narrative — above all the critique of modernity — and rejects others, and is not a perennialist but a believing Catholic. The red thread, in Sedgwick's reading, is the critique of modernity and not a shared metaphysics. The interview is auto-captioned and unchecked against the audio, so this is paraphrase.

events.title: 'War for Eternity'
events.text: Benjamin Teitelbaum's ethnographic account links Bannon, Dugin and Olavo de Carvalho through Traditionalism, based on extensive Bannon interviews; reviewers dispute how coherent or consequential the 'network' really is — the book's stronger claims are the author's, not consensus. Interviewed on the Pill Pod podcast on or about 8 January 2021, Teitelbaum named his own object 'rightist' or political traditionalism — a term he says the Traditionalist author Charles Upton, himself strongly opposed to the figures the book studies, asked him to use, and which draws the same religious/political line this chronology draws; Upton is carried in the sibling cronologia/tariqa project, not here. In the same interview he set his own limit on the network thesis: that Traditionalism may be, as he put it, the fancy language of people who are populist but dislike thinking of themselves as populist, and that deciding otherwise would require a degree of mind-reading he is not comfortable with as a scholar. He also reported the reception — Bannon considering his own sections faithful, Dugin liking the book, and Olavo de Carvalho answering it with videos attacking him by name — and noted that the US and European editions carry different subtitles. Auto-captioned interview, unchecked against the audio: paraphrase, not quotation. A second reviewer datum, read in full for this entry: Luke Harding's Guardian review of 5 June 2020, headlined 'starstruck by Steve Bannon', finds the book good on Bannon but weak on Dugin and Russian politics; presses that Teitelbaum refers to Bannon chummily as 'Steve' and that it is never entirely clear whether the author shares his subjects' extreme views or regards them as 'ethnographic curiosities'; and rejects the Dugin-inspired-Putin framing — on Harding's account the Kremlin promoted Dugin because his theories suited Putin's great-power project, a mission owing nothing to Evola or Guénon. The same review supplies a printed figure for the interviews behind the book: twenty hours of conversation with Bannon in 2018–19.

events.title: The 'Box Essencial Guénon'
events.text: A boxed set of eight Guénon titles newly translated from the French appears in Brazil. Felipe Souza, writing on Mark Sedgwick's Traditionalists blog on 23 October 2023, records the 'Essential René Guénon Box' as released in 2022 by Editora Bismillah 'in collaboration with Editorial Estrela da Manhã'; the ICLS launch livestream 'Por que ler René Guénon?' presents Editorial Estrela da Manhã as the publisher, with Marcelo Cipolla as the project's editor and Marcos Monteiro as translator. The two accounts of the imprint are recorded, not reconciled. Souza adds that the quality of the rival IRGET translations 'is a subject of controversy'. The launch stream's own date of 11 March 2022 is uploader metadata (to verify).

events.title: Sedgwick's 'Traditionalism'
events.text: The analytic synthesis of the philosophy of Guénon, Evola and Schuon and its applications — the school historicized by the scholar who mapped it. Presenting the book to a general audience at the UnHerd Club in Westminster on 28 July 2023, Sedgwick said that he is not himself a Traditionalist, that he has been mistaken for one, and that at points in his life he has found the ideas attractive — a self-disclosure worth recording in a subject where affiliation language is contested.

figures.name: René Guénon
figures.role: Founder-metaphysician of the school; his 1921–1951 corpus defines 'Tradition', the critique of modernity and the primacy of metaphysics; Paris, then Cairo from 1930.

figures.name: Ananda K. Coomaraswamy
figures.role: Ceylonese-British art historian and Boston MFA curator; after his 1932 metaphysical turn, the school's comparativist of traditional art, Vedanta and Platonism.

figures.name: Frithjof Schuon (as author)
figures.role: The school's most systematic expositor: 'The Transcendent Unity of Religions' (1948) and some twenty further books on the religio perennis. His order, the Maryamiyya, is the sibling tariqa project's subject. A short interview published by his own publisher, World Wisdom, has him state the position in compressed form: the metaphysics is Hinduism while the religion and the framework are Islam; syncretism is an error, though a certain syncretism is possible in pure esoterism; religion is an adaptation able to save everyone where philosophy cannot; and metaphysical truth, not religion alone, is what draws him to God. The footage carries no date and the publisher's page could not be reached, so when it was filmed is undetermined (to verify), and the captions are poor enough that this is paraphrase and never quotation.

figures.name: Julius Evola
figures.role: The political adaptation: warrior-regal Traditionalism ('Revolt Against the Modern World', 1934), against Guénon's priority of the sacerdotal; never a fascist party member, self-styled 'superfascista' at his 1951 trial (acquitted); chief ideologue of the postwar Italian radical right per scholarship, revived by the 2010s alt-right.

figures.name: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
figures.role: The academic institutionalizer: Gifford Lectures 1981 ('Knowledge and the Sacred') — first Muslim Gifford lecturer per the Gifford records — 'sacred science' and Islamic environmentalism. He left Temple University in 1984 for George Washington University as University Professor of Islamic Studies and, per his official biography, that same year founded the Foundation for Traditional Studies, 'promoting traditional wisdom and publishing the journal Sophia'. His standing inside Schuon's order is the tariqa project's subject, not this one's.

figures.name: Martin Lings (as author)
figures.role: Keeper of Oriental manuscripts at the British Museum/Library; the prize-winning 'Muhammad' (1983) and Shakespeare-as-sacred-art studies.

figures.name: Titus Burckhardt
figures.role: Theorist of sacred art ('Sacred Art in East and West', 1958; 'Art of Islam', 1976); Fez and Chartres monographs; UNESCO consultant on Fez.

figures.name: Huston Smith
figures.role: American comparative religion's public face ('The Religions of Man', 1958); openly perennialist from 'Forgotten Truth' (1976) under Schuon's influence — the bridge into US classrooms.

figures.name: Marco Pallis
figures.role: Mountaineer-author ('Peaks and Lamas', 1939); Tibetan Buddhism's Traditionalist interpreter and Guénon translator.

figures.name: Lord Northbourne (Walter James)
figures.role: Agronomist peer who coined 'organic farming' ('Look to the Land', 1940) and later translated Guénon and Burckhardt — the school's link to the organic movement.

figures.name: Jean-Louis Michon
figures.role: French scholar-translator of Moroccan Sufism and Islamic art; UNESCO cultural-heritage work in Morocco; perennialist author.

figures.name: Aldous Huxley
figures.role: Contrast figure: his 'The Perennial Philosophy' (1945) popularized the phrase in a universalist-mystical sense unconnected to — and rejected by — the Guénonian school.

figures.name: Mircea Eliade
figures.role: The contested case: he read Guénon and Evola in interwar Romania; Sedgwick treats him as a concealed 'soft' Traditionalist, while Davide Marino (Aries, 2022) and the earlier Italian reassessment call the affinity a myth — the site records the debate, not a verdict.

figures.name: Mark Sedgwick & Wouter Hanegraaff
figures.role: The historians of the school: Sedgwick (Aarhus; 'Against the Modern World' 2004, 'Traditionalism' 2023, the Traditionalists blog) and Hanegraaff (Amsterdam; Traditionalism as 'religionism' within esotericism studies).

organizations.name: Études Traditionnelles (journal)
organizations.relation: The school's house journal — Le Voile d'Isis (1889) renamed under Guénon's dominance; monthly then quarterly, with a 1940–45 wartime gap, until its 1992 close. Digitized runs survive at IAPSOP.

organizations.name: Sophia Perennis (publisher)
organizations.relation: James R. Wetmore's press — publisher of the English 'Collected Works of René Guénon' (23 volumes); described on Sedgwick's blog as the leading US Guénonian-Traditionalist publisher. Founding year still to pin down.

organizations.name: World Wisdom (publisher)
organizations.relation: The 'Library of Perennial Philosophy' — main English-language publisher of Schuon, Burckhardt, Pallis and Nasr; participant-run, labeled sympathetic. Shared with the tariqa project's story.

organizations.name: Fons Vitae (publisher)
organizations.relation: Aisha Gray Henry's nonprofit press — Sufism, the Ghazali series, Lings's works. The founding year remains genuinely unresolved across sources: Wikipedia's narrative gives 1984 (tracing Gray Henry's publishing back through the Quinta Essentia imprint she ran at the Islamic Texts Society, later transferred to Fons Vitae), its infobox gives 1996, and IRS/nonprofit records for 'Fons Vitae of Kentucky' give a formation year of 2000. The Quinta Essentia predecessor explains much of the split between the earlier and later dates.
organizations.notes: Founding year unresolved: 1984 (Wikipedia narrative / Quinta Essentia lineage), 1996 (Wikipedia infobox), 2000 (Kentucky nonprofit formation).

organizations.name: Temenos Academy
organizations.relation: Grew from the Temenos review (1980, Kathleen Raine and colleagues); initially housed in the Prince of Wales's Institute of Architecture, with Charles — now King Charles III — as patron since its founding. The institutional face of the school's arts-and-imagination wing; royal 'sympathies' beyond the documented patronage are reported only as attributed commentary.

organizations.name: Foundation for Traditional Studies / journal Sophia
organizations.relation: The school's academic-facing organ. Nasr founded it in 1984 — the year he moved to George Washington University — 'promoting traditional wisdom and publishing the journal Sophia', per his official biography. Nasr's Sophia is not the Springer / University of Melbourne 'Sophia: International Journal of Philosophy and Traditions' (founded 1962): a name collision, not a relation. Who among Schuon's order sat on the Foundation and wrote for the journal is the tariqa project's material, cross-referenced there rather than repeated here — a deliberate difference of scope between the two datasets, not a disagreement about the facts.
organizations.notes: Two dates on one card: 1984 is the Foundation's founding; the journal came later — the Matheson Trust dates Sophia's semi-annual run 'since 1995'. The Washington, DC seat is flagged to verify: neither cited source states an address.

disambiguation.note: The word 'perennialism' is a collision zone, and the school's political receptions are contested. These cards keep the lines straight; every characterization is attributed.

items.title: Guénonian Traditionalism ≠ Huxley's perennialism
items.text: Huxley's 1945 anthology is experiential-mystical universalism, indifferent to orthodoxy and initiation; the Guénonians insist truth is transmitted only through orthodox revealed traditions and generally rejected Huxley-style syncretism. Same phrase, two lineages.

items.title: ≠ 'philosophia perennis' in academic philosophy
items.text: Steuco (1540) and Leibniz used the term for a continuity thesis inside Western philosophy and Christian Platonism, and neo-Scholastics applied it to Thomism — neither is the Guénonian doctrine.

items.title: The school ≠ the order
items.text: This site covers the school of ideas — books, journals, reception. The initiatic and organizational history of Schuon's Maryamiyya order is the sibling cronologia/tariqa project; events belong to exactly one of the two.

items.title: Evola's line ≠ Schuon's line
items.text: Evola politicized Tradition — regal, activist, with a postwar neofascist reception running to Dugin and the alt-right; Schuon's line is religious-metaphysical and non-political. Guénon himself criticized Evola's inversions. Every claim placing a modern actor in this lineage is attributed to the scholar or actor making it.

items.title: Eliade is a debate, not a datum
items.text: Mark Sedgwick reads Mircea Eliade as a concealed 'soft' Traditionalist ('Against the Modern World', 2004) — a reading he restated in 2022 even while granting that Eliade's references to Guénon grew critical after the 1950s ('his early soft Traditionalism is still found in his later work'). Against this, Davide Marino ('Mircea Eliade and René Guénon', Aries, 2022) argues the 'myth of affinity' arose from misunderstandings and that Traditionalism and Eliade's hermeneutics are theoretically irreconcilable; the earlier Italian reassessment gathered in Arcella, Pisi and Scagno's 'Confronto con Mircea Eliade' (Jaca Book, 1998) had already questioned the traditionalist reading. The site records the debate, not a verdict.

items.title: The royal reception is attributed commentary
items.text: King Charles III's Temenos patronage (documented since 1990, and self-disclosed in his 2006 Sacred Web address) and 'Harmony' (2010) are read by commentators — Sedgwick, Commonweal, The American Conservative, The Spectator — as showing Traditionalist and Nasrian influence; the book cites no Traditionalist sources, and no membership or self-identification exists. What is self-disclosed is reading, patronage and praise; Sedgwick, reporting the 2006 address, wrote expressly that it did not clarify the Prince's own personal position. Sympathies are reported as the commentators' claims — never as affiliation.

items.title: 'Founder' or 'developer': how Coomaraswamy gets described
items.text: Popular reprints and introductions call Ananda K. Coomaraswamy a co-founder — the Sutra Journal reprint of his 'True Art' (October 2015) says in its editorial introduction, not in Coomaraswamy's own text, that he 'is regarded as one of the three founders of Perennialism, also called the Traditionalist School', alongside Guénon and Schuon. This chronology uses the framing of its own summary: Guénon founded the current, Coomaraswamy and Schuon developed it — the school's formation is usually described as an intellectual convergence rather than an act of foundation, and Schuon (b. 1907) belongs to a later generation than Guénon (b. 1886) and Coomaraswamy (b. 1877). The sibling cronologia/tariqa dataset describes him instead as one of the school's 'three founding authors'; the divergence is recorded here rather than resolved, since it turns on what 'founding' is taken to mean. Note also that Ananda K. Coomaraswamy (1877-1947), the art historian, is not his son Rama P. Coomaraswamy — a distinction the sibling cronologia projects depend on.

items.title: The outlet's framing is not the scholar's claim
items.text: UnHerd published its 28 July 2023 interview with Mark Sedgwick under the headline 'Traditionalism: the philosophy behind Putin's war'. In the interview itself Sedgwick says that Alexander Dugin is not part of Putin's circle and that Putin has a brain of his own, while granting that Dugin exerts influence and enjoys something like a forbidden-guru status. The headline is the outlet's; the qualifications are the scholar's. The interviewer is bylined only 'UnHerd Staff' and is never named on air, so the questions are attributed to the outlet and not to a person. Wherever a scholarly source reaches this chronology through a partisan outlet, the two voices are cited separately — the same rule that keeps commentators' readings off the affiliation record in the card above. The interview is auto-captioned, so Sedgwick's positions are paraphrased here and never quoted.

items.title: A different genealogy — and a third Rama
items.text: Not every 'esoteric roots of the new right' account is a compressed version of this one. The Brazilian programme Paz e Bem #1294 (10 June 2022), in which Mauro Lopes interviews Prof. Neide Miele — a Universidade Federal da Paraíba academic in Ciências das Religiões and the founder of that programme's journal Religare, an affiliation confirmed from the university's own journals portal and not from the broadcast, which never names her institution — traces a line from Antoine Fabre d'Olivet and Alexandre Saint-Yves d'Alveydre through Édouard Schuré to Papus and to Julius Evola, and joins Dugin, Olavo de Carvalho and Steve Bannon to it not by initiatic descent but by a shared hatred of the French Revolution and the Enlightenment. René Guénon is not named in the programme at all, in any spelling; Fabre d'Olivet, Saint-Yves, Papus and Blavatsky are in turn absent from both of the scholarly interviews this chronology draws on. The two accounts do not overlap, so this one is recorded as Prof. Miele's attributed narrative out of French occultist historiography — neither corroborating nor contradicting the lineage charted here — and 'Evola descends from Saint-Yves' is never this site's claim. The programme is progressive-Catholic and left in perspective and its present-day readings, including calling the removal of Dilma Rousseff a coup, are hers and dated. One further trap it sets: the Rama of that literature is the mythical Vedic figure, a third referent alongside Ananda K. Coomaraswamy, this chronology's figure, and his son Rama P. Coomaraswamy, who belongs to the sibling tariqa and fsspx projects. Its auto-captions mangle every proper name in the genealogy, so all of them are reconstructions from context and none is quoted.

Solid edges are direct intellectual discipleship or collaboration; dashed edges are influence, reception or cross-links, always attributed to the scholar or actor asserting them. Julius Evola's political adaptation and Aldous Huxley's same-named 'Perennial Philosophy' are set apart as separate lines that are NOT continuations of the Guénonian school.
